# Meeting Etiquette [👔](https://emojipedia.org/necktie/)

### Proposing Agenda Items…

* **Anyone** can propose small-ish items  
* Ask/discuss with the group when to schedule  
  * Folks may add to meetings on-the-fly (as time permits)  
* [Follow the CNCF Code of Conduct](https://github.com/cncf/foundation/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md)  
* *The TAG can also schedule meetings other days per request. Reach out to the chairs or **\#tag-runtime** on the [CNCF Slack](https://communityinviter.com/apps/cloud-native/cncf) for more information.*

### Agenda: 📑

* [Open Cluster Management (OCM)](https://github.com/open-cluster-management-io/ocm) project update.   
  * [Presentation Slides](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pw2DjfcrstBJ5kOUwiO1pu30qAa-BAg-/view?usp=drive_link).  
  * Presenter: Mike Ng (@mikeshng)

Notes:

* OCM  
  * Open cluster management  
* CNCF Sandbox project  
  * Onboarded 5 years ago  
* ![][image10]  
* ![][image11]  
* Hub & Spoke model  
  * Pull Model from Hub  
* Placement  
  * Scheduling of resources to clusters based on set of criteria  
  * Placement decision  
  *    
*   
  * ![][image12]  
* Workload Distribution  
  * ManifestWork API  
  * ![][image13]  
* This is about Workload Placement and Scheduling  
  * Not cluster management  
  * Clusters exist or are created, and then register with OCM for workloads  
* Now supports AI workload Scheduling  
* Argo CD Integration  
* ![][image14]  
* ApplicationSet Controller moves to the Spoke Cluster  
* Argocd-agent repo  
* Can use OCM to deploy the agent  
* Then move to using the argo agent  
*    
*    
* Governance Policy Framework Add-on  
  * Integration with OPA Gatekeeper  
* Cluster Proxy Add-on  
  * Apiserver-network-proxy  
  * Ie. “Konnectivity” support  
  * ![][image15]  
* kubeVela integration  
* “Hosted Mode”  
  * Cluster with multiple hubs?  
  * Delegate the OCM aspect outside of the cluster  
  * Cluster doesn’t run the agent  
  * Hub reaches out directly  
  * Can we still konnectivity though? Unclear need to follow-up  
* Multi-cluster Controlplane  
  * Multiple OCM instances in different namespaces  
  * Liteweight controlplane  
  * Allow to manage many other clusters  
  * A “hub of hubs”

## Notes:

* ComposeFS First  
* “Opportunistically sharing verified image filesystem  
  * OCI, images, etc.  
  * Not like layers  
  * Things are shared  
* “Reliability of disk images, flexibility of files  
* Read-only, meant to be used with another FS  
* Composefs in RHEL9, RHEL10  
* Storing any kind of images  
* OCI are tight integration planned  
* Compose filesystems  
* Mount with mount command  
* Checksum is “fs-verity” checksum  
  * Kernel enforced checksum  
  * (Different from sha256)  
* Mount time can succeed  
* Composefs is small file  
  * Never use sha256  
  * Everything is fs-verity digest  
  * Composefs metadata file  
* Used in OStree  
  * RHEL / Fedora  
* The rest of the file system is represented in object files  
* So that’s the OS level.  
* But also targeting OCI / Containers level  
  * Currently basic support in podman  
* Container images:  
  * High density due to file sharing  
  * Validation of images  
  * Signature of images  
    * Integration with cosign future possibility  
* Container storage model:  
  * Files checksummed so easy to find existing files for “sharing”  
* One image  
  * Necessarily takes the same space as traditional OCI  
* Multiple images:  
  * Sharing more granular than image layer  
  * So can share much of the same layer across multiple layers  
  * If only one file change, much less space used  
* Also execution based  
  * Less memory usage at runtime as well  
  * Only one copy of the file  
* ![][image34]  
*    
* Sigstore verifies composefs digest  
  * Then fs-verity verifies the rest  
* Path to ecosystem  
  * Change OCI image  
  * Erofs mount per layer today  
  * Could squish the layer  
  * Control in ostree / podman  
* Build time  
  * Nothing needed at build time  
  * Only the signature / digest support  
  * Which can be from a separate tool  
  * Ie: don’t have to change docker build  
  * Not re-inventing images, still bundle of tar files with layers  
* Run time  
  * Composefs on the runtime side, pull down any image and take advantage of the on-disk format. On-the-wire format doesn’t change.

* **BootC**  
  * USe OCI standard, layer, container registries, signing, testing, gitops to build linux systems  
*    
* What everyone knows, and does today. Powerful:  
* ![][image35]  
*     
* Make a container bootable\!  
* ![][image36]   
*    
* All linux systems now driven with gitops pipelines  
*    
* Make the linux administrator experience aligned with container experience  
  * Apply container skills to OS  
* Role of bootc:  
  * Fetch, deploy bootable container images  
* Persistence:  
  * /etc and /var are default “persistent volumes” analogous / persistent state  
* A/B fashion, sharing state and single filesystem  
* If you can put it in OCI bootc will boot it  
* Requires:  
  * A kernel in the OCI image  
  * Nothing imposed at runtime  
* Uses the same OCI but re-uses filesystem, not all config (like exposing ports, etc.)  
* How does this make it bootable  
* Everywhere you can use podman, you can transfer those skills to baremetal booting containers  
*    
* Bootc install to disk or filesystem  
  * Builds filesystem, partitions, etc.  
*   
*

Notes:

* **K0s**  
  * Intro  
    * Super easy to put in any infrastructure and “Just work”  
    * Just run in and kubernetes is there  
    * Single binary  
  * Single Binary  
    * Kernel modules loaded  
    * OS / k0s decoupled  
    * Cgroups, etc.  
  * All components included  
    *   
    * Containerd, kube-router, Calico, etcd and Kine  
    * (can swap with your own runtime, but not included in k0s)  
  * Flexible deployment  
    * Control plane vs. worker nodes separate  
    * Reverse tunnel between  
    * Konnectivity  
      * Agent on worker nodes  
      * Server on control plane nodes  
      * Common practice these days  
        * E.g. azure AKS uses konnectivity as well  
      * Can put worker nodes in private DC, and control plane can run elsewhere in public cloud  
        * Can work worker nodes behind firewall  
    * Controlplane  
      * No workloads possible on control nodes by default  
      * Can override this (if really want to)  
    * Single-node version  
      * Swapout sqlite/kine in this mode as well  
  * Autopilot  
    * Cluster level upgrade  
    * Automate cluster lifecycle  
    * CRD Plan  
      * Set version  
      * Update controllers, etc.   
    * Operator  
      * Coordinates which node to restart  
      * Upgrade is restart k0s binary  
      * But operator does this in the right order  
  * Edge  
    * Controllers somewhere else  
    * Workers pure worker nodes (control plane not in an edge site)  
  * Simplicity of operations:  
* ![][image37]  
*    
* System requirements:  
* ![][image38]  
* “Minimum”  
* Clearly, etcd., more node count etc. affects this  
* ![][image39]  
*    
* Demo:  
  * K0s controller install  
    * Installs systemd unit  
  * K0s start  
  * K0s  
    * Central process  
    * Glorified watchdog for all the processes  
  * Control plane:  
    * No kubelet  
    * So no nodes until worker nodes are created  
  * Workers  
    * Token create –role=worker  
    * (analogous to kubeadm)  
    * K0s install worker –token-file \</etc/k0s.token\>  
    * K0s start  
  * Node ready in \~20s  
* Community  
  * \~440k installs as of nov. 2024  
* Sandbox goals  
  * Improve governance during this time  
  * Improve community aspects  
* ![][image40]  
*  

**Drasi**: [Drasi-CNCF Runtime TAG presentation](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/16EFUOIYDUjq1OzlCTlgbQBgKAHJUaSCB8CO3_ikK64E/edit?usp=sharing)

* Project that allows you to detect changes in Data and generate an event.  
* The usual way to do it is to poll a database.

				![][image41]

* For things I just want to do a thing to do something if data changes  
  * To address the overhead of many changes  
  * Doing it right it very complicated  
    * How do you scale? Etc (it’s not a trivial problem)  
* Drasi \-\> Change driven architecture  
* ![][image42]  
* Drasi has a source SDK (Postgres, cosmos, sql server, K8s \- experimental)  
* Drasi also has a reaction SDK  
* ![][image43]  
* Interesting aspect of Drasi is continuous queries (not a new concept)  
* ![][image44]  
* Can match “set” of things that change  
* Uses “Cypher” queries  
  * Cypher is a graph query language.  
  * Useful for “Heirarchical” data  
  * “Queries across databases”

Notes:

* Kro  
  * “Building with kubernetes is embracing it as a platform”  
    * Build CRs  
    * Build Controllers  
    * K8S as foundational as a platform effort  
  * How do we make this easier  
  * ACK  
    * Aws controllers for kubernetes  
    * Like google/azure have similars  
    * Drive cloud resource management  
    * Infrastructure as kubernetes config  
  * Kro (pronounced: crow)  
    * Managing multiple resources  
    * Timing of config  
    * Injecting across resources  
  * Introduce a single CRD called Resource Group  
    * Then we can manage all other resources  
    * We allow very complex used cases  
  * Any resource can be part of a resource group  
    * Any CR/controller can be part  
    * Including load balancer for example  
  * Any cloud is supported  
  * Kro itself is an operator  
  * The ResourceGroup that we define is created by kro  
    * Kro itself will dynamically create new CRDs  
    * Will also deploy a microcontroller to manage that new CRD  
  * [https://kro.run/docs/getting-started/deploy-a-resource-group](https://kro.run/docs/getting-started/deploy-a-resource-group)  
    * Top-level: ResourceGroup  
    * Input: CEL expressions  
    * Output: resources  
      * Also use CEL expressions  
      * Allows to references other resources within the expressions

Notes:

* ![][image72]

* ![][image73]  
*    
* Testing and releasing regularly:  
  * Baremetal operator  
  * Cluster api provider metal  
  * IPAM  
  * Ironic-image  
* Ironic  
  * Handles the baseboard management controllers (BMC)  
  * Handles the provisioning agent (IPA)  
* Bare Metal Operator  
  * Tells ironic what to do  
* IP address manager:  
  * Kubernetes native IPAM  
  * For scenarios where users can’t rely on DHCP for physical interface IPs  
* BMC:  
  * Support BMC specific management protocols  
  * As well as standard RedFish and IPMI  
* ![][image74]  
*    
* ![][image75]  
*    
* ![][image76]  
*    
* Want to be the “Go-to” bare metal provisioners in CNCF  
*    
* ![][image77]  
*    
* Openshift & Ericsson highlight  
*  ![][image78]  
*    
* After sandbox, created a lot of infra and structure for community, governance, security, meetups.   
*   
* ![][image79]   
*    
* Will soon reach 200 recordings on youtube  
*     
* Questions:  
* Maintainers?  
  * 15  
  * Mostly across two companies  
  * RedHat 50%  
  * Ericsson 50%  
  * Are some emeritus maintainers from other orgs  
* Contributions?  
  * Across many others  
* How do you handle embargoed issues?  
  * Documented, some can be handled publicly, some can be handled privately  
  * Discussion behind closed doors  
  * After embargoed lifted, then can open up.  
  * Is documented in security document  
* What is release cadence?  
  * CAPM3 Metal3:  
    * Every time there is a cluster api release  
    * 4 month release cycle  
  * IP-address manager:  
    * Following CAPM3 (CAPI) releases  
  * Baremetal:  
    * Decide in community discussion  
  * Ironic-image:  
    * Following Ironic upstream release  
    * If community decides there can be extra releases  
* Do you have to follow new kubernetes versions?  
  * Guiding principle is CAPI  
  * Muhammad ghaffar is in CAPI release team as well  
  * Do a CAPI as soon as possible within a week of kubernetes  
  * Metal3 does as well within a week of patch release  
* Current test infra owned by ericsson?  
  * Party provided  
  * Plan to move to community resources? (Yes)  
  * Need quite a bit of resources to simulate baremetal behaviors  
  * End-to-end test is provided by ericsson: openstack cloud  
  * Vendor neutrality declaration  
  * Ongoing work  
* Releases:  
  * regarding BMO releases: Community decided we do 3 minor releases of Baremetal operator per year.   
  * v0.4.0 released  Aug 30, 2023  
  * v0.5.0 released Jan, 2024  
  * v0.6.0 released Apr 17  
  *   
* CAPM3 \- how different from other existing cluster-api sigs providers?  
  * Difference:  
    * Support virtual media booting and ipxi and redfish virtualmedia  
    * WIP support redfish uefi http booting in the future [https://github.com/metal3-io/metal3-docs/pull/459/files](https://github.com/metal3-io/metal3-docs/pull/459/files)   
    * So supports more methods of booting than others  
  * Agent can add value:  
    * Preconfig of machines?  
    * Cleaning  
    * Wider set of tools  
    * Not just pixie booting  
  * Distro independence  
    * Nothing metal3 specific needs to be in disk image  
    * Not relying on specific linux distro  
    * Key feature of two-stage provisioning process, 1st stage handled by the agent  
* Tinkerbell collaboration  
  * Very different  
  * Metal3 build on  BMO and Ironic  
  * Not really applies  
*    
* DEMO  
* ![][image80]  
*    
* ![][image81]  
* Wanted to show hardware upgrade use-case (Not K8s upgrade)  
* Regular K8s upgrade is done by CAPI providers as that is a  common operation  
* Real life use-case, baremetal cluster, wanted to swap out the machine without disturbing anything  
* Not that common of a use case to change physical machines .  
* Cloud provider based providers typically don’t swap out hardware and put in a new one directly  
* Metal3 can do this type of  control plane node and worker node replacement   
*    
* What kind of coupling is there between k8s version in CAPI and the node version?  
  * Not tight coupling, supports what CAPI supports  
  * Because Metal3 can deliver any disk image it is up to CAPI what K8s upgrades are supported

* Confidential VMs  
  * Main memory of VM is encrypted within the CPU

* AMD / Intel CPU extensions  
  * ARM has a spec no implementation yet  
* Most cloud providers offer this  
* Bringing this to Cloud Native  
* Constellation:  
  * VM based (entire nodes)  
* Contrast:  
  * PODS in CVMs  
* ![][image83]  
* Leveraging Kata Containers  
* “Confidential Containers”  
  * Sandbox project  
  * K8s Container Runtime  
* If baremetal, this is straightforward  
* Nested VM  
  * Kvm does not support w/ confidential computing directly  
  * Azure hyperv only for now  
* If not nested  
  * ![][image84]  
* Kata shim  
  * Can use via remote hypervisor  
* Support for NVIDIA H100 as well  
  * Useful for AI workloads  
  * Need H100 available  
  * And confidential VM (CVM) available  
  *   
* ![][image85]  
* Protect against thread model  
  * Isolate workload from entire infrastructure  
  * Reduce trust in the cloud  
* ![][image86]  
*    
* How do I verify:  
  * “Start in confidential container runtime”  
  * Don’t trust kubernetes at all  
  * Only the pod is trusted in this model (through confidential container)  
  * Attestation scalable  
    * Attestation service  
    * Verifies all the pods  
    * Agent runs and enforces  
  * Coordinator Container  
    * Validate to API server  
  * Then: Third Party  
    * Can be verified through the attestation  
* ![][image87]  
* [https://github.com/confidential-containers/cloud-api-adaptor](https://github.com/confidential-containers/cloud-api-adaptor)  
* For Cloud Provider Support:  
  * NEed one of:  
    * nested CVMs  
    * PeerPod: confidential VM runs separately, split at the kata-shim  
    * Baremetal  
  * Each have tradeoffs  
  * Baremetal has the least amount of tradeoffs  
* Demo:  
  * [https://docs.edgeless.systems/contrast/examples/emojivoto](https://docs.edgeless.systems/contrast/examples/emojivoto)  
* [https://github.com/edgelesssys/contrast](https://github.com/edgelesssys/contrast)

### Scribes: ✍️

* Stephen Rust

### Notes:

* Romil Bhardwaj presenting  
  * Post-doc at UC Berkeley  
* SkyPilot: Run AI Anywhere  
  * Find GPU capacity where avail  
  * More cost effective  
  * AI is expensive in the cloud  
* Typical:  
  * Multiple clouds  
  * Regions, zones  
  * Choose exact GPU  
  * Provision  
  * Transfer all your data  
  * Setup your container, etc.  
  * Still manage all the jobs, manage all the nodes, manage all the clusters across clouds  
* Challenges:  
  * “Hundreds of Choices”  
  * “Deal with Availability” \- GPU in short supply  
  * “Manage with Infra  
  * Cost

  ![][image97]

* Companies spend 80% of their total capital raised  
  * Mostly on GPU cost  
  * Cloud costs  
* Skypilot Vision:  
  * Simple and Cost-effective AI

![][image98]

* Skypilot  
  * Intercloud broker  
  * Saving Cost  
  * Maximizing Availability  
* Pick best location  
  * Provision  
  * Run  
  * Cleanup

![][image99]

* mistral.ai used Skypilot to deploy some of their models

* But: Why actually use Skypilot

![][image100]

![][image101]

* Manual steps / commands converted to yaml  
* Also specify resources required  
  * “Type” of GPU  
* File mounts for data

![][image102]

* “Best” means lowest cost, today

![][image103]

* Developers:  
  * Workloads are not typically latency sensitive  
  * Don’t care about regions necessarily  
  * Just care about cost  
* Multi-cloud  
  * Can bring your own cluster as well  
  * Can do on-prem as well cloud spillover  
  * Will allocate from cloud if on-prem is busy

* “Sky launch” list

![][image104]

* GPU requirement filters the types of clusters available

![][image105]

* Cost maintained for clouds in a “catalog”  
* Skypilot references this catalog to determine the cost

* How to choose “best”:  
  * Today, cost  
  * Can also choose based on carbon emissions

![][image106]

* Can do “Spot VMs”  
  * Cheap, but unreliable  
* Skypilot offers a “managed spot instance manager”  
  * If pre-empted, re-launch wherever capacity available

*   
  * Up to the application to 

![][image107]

* Question: training job can take days. How does checkpointing work, to move jobs when pre-empted.  
  * State is stored on object buckets  
  * Cloud buckets are used as persistent storage  
  * How often is checkpointing:  
    * Application must perform checkpointing on its own  
    * No managed checkpointing  
    * So if checkpoint once a day, you may lose up to 1 day, if pre-empted  
  * GPU makes auto checkpointing without application awareness difficult

![][image108]

* Bring your own kubernetes in beta. “On-prem”  
* Customers want SSH access to the workload  
  * Run “ssh proxy” mod in-cluster  
  * GPU status  
  * Update the run  
  * Used to using “slurm” in academic environments  
  * Hard to abstract what users are doing  
  * SSH access was the best method to handle all use-cases

![][image109]

* Storage Options:  
  * Can fuse mount  
  * Or can copy data on the start

![][image110]

* Nvidia contacts possible: reach out after the meeting  
* DRA (dynamic resource allocator)  
  * Dynamically change GPU partitioning

* Workload Edge / locations  
  * Latency not as concerning  
  * Location is, for data governance / compliance (gdpr, etc.)  
  * Keep data in-house  
  * HTTP request latency is high anyway (5s vs. 5.2s not a big deal)

#### Scribes: ✍️

Notes:

* Flame:  
  * Distributed workloads:  
    * For AI (simplify dist workloads), Quant, Web, Sentient.   
    * Quant: speedup algorithm: eg: monte carlo  
    * Web: simplify/speed elastic workload, crawler/encoder  
    * Sensient: cross language library, python/rust  
* Architecture:  
  * ![][image111]  
* Client \-\>   
  * Submit tasks until we have enough tasks  
* \-\> Flame Session Manager  
  * Support several policies  
*  \-\> Flame Executor Manager   
  * Agent on worker node  
    * Different shims in pod  
      * Stdio  
      * Wasm  
      * Grpc  
    * Execute directly applications directly into pod, not offloading to any other runtime.  
  * Flame operator  
    * Different policies  
  * Flame autoscaler  
* Flame SDK  
  * Flame client  
    * Connect / create sessions / run tasks  
  * Flame service  
    * Callbacks execute tasks for sessions  
  * ![][image112]

* Flame Python SDK  
  * In-progress  
  * Transfer function  
* What is SDK used for?  
  * Two parts  
    * Task invoke executed on several nodes  
    * Client single invocation  
    * Server is distributed / 1000 nodes  
      * To do parallel execution  
    * Can re-use server side code  
  * Following the import for the tasks w/ binaries  
  * Can have re-usable server-side task components that clients can execute  
* Session Manager Details:  
  * ![][image113]  
  * Scheduler  
* Executor Manager Details:  
  * ![][image114]  
  * Shared cache  
  * Disriued cache  
* Demo:  
  * Rust client  
  * PI client  
    * Running  kubernetes (could run anywhere, as long as can talk to server)  
  * PI server  
  * Running in minikube  
  * `Flmctl`  
    * Command line   
  * ![][image115]  
  * Calculate the pi for each task  
  * Logs for flame executor manager show the task invocations  
  * Pi client  
    * Via APIs:  
    * Creates session  
    * Submits all the tasks  
    * Waits for completion  
    * Gather output from remote  
  * Pi server  
    * Generate random data  
    * Perform calculuation  
    * Print result                                      
* Need client and server for every problem you’re trying to solve  
  * Would write own server for your problem  
  * And write your client  
  * Server performs the work  
  * Client submits tasks and processes results / does something with result  
* Demo Matrix Multiplication  
  * ![][image116]  
  * Can carefully craft process, to operate only on specific data that we need to  
  * Client submits to server to use compute processing  
  * Don’t have to calculate on laptop, etc.

    * Not CRD support, this is more internal data structure

* [Usernetes Gen2 (Kubernetes in Rootless Docker) \- Akihiro Suda](https://github.com/rootless-containers/usernetes/discussions/304)  
  Slides [https://github.com/AkihiroSuda/AkihiroSuda/blob/master/slides/2023/20231027%20%5BCNCF%20TAG-Runtime%5D%20Usernetes%20Gen2.pdf](https://github.com/AkihiroSuda/AkihiroSuda/blob/master/slides/2023/20231027%20%5BCNCF%20TAG-Runtime%5D%20Usernetes%20Gen2.pdf) 

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [suda.kyoto@gmail.com](mailto:suda.kyoto@gmail.com)

Notes:

* Usernetes [https://github.com/rootless-containers/usernetes](https://github.com/rootless-containers/usernetes)   
  * Rootless Kubernetes  
    * Even if an attacker has escaped from a Pod, or gained an access to kubelet API, the attacker still cannot gain the root privilege of the node  
  * Implemented by putting kubelet, CRI, OCI, CNI, etc. in a user namespace  
    * UserNS: Linux kernel’s feature that maps a non-root user to a fake root  
      (the root privilege is limited inside the namespace)  
  * Multi-node networking is possible with VXLAN  
  * History  
    * Began in 2018  
      * As old as Rootless Docker (pre-release at that time) and Rootless Podman  
    * The changes to Kubernetes was merged in Kubernetes v1.22  
      (Aug 2021\)  
      * Feature gate: “KubeletInUserNamespace” (Alpha)  
    * The feature gate was also adopted by:  
      * kind         (with Rootless Docker or Rootless Podman)  
      * Minikube (with Rootless Docker or Rootless Podman)  
      * K3s  
  * Usernetes Gen 1 vs Gen 2

|  | Gen 1 (2018-2023) | Gen 2 (2023-) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Host dependency** | RootlessKit | Rootless Docker,Rootless Podman, orRootless nerdctl(contaiNERD CTL) |
| **Supports kubeadm** | No | Yes |
| **Supports multi-node** | Yes, but practically No,due to complexity | Yes |
| **Supports hostPath volumes** | Yes | Yes, for most paths, but needs an extra config |

    * Gen 1: “The hard way”  
    * Gen 2: Similar to \`kind\` and minikube, but supports real multi-node  
  * Usage

| \# Bootstrap the first node make up make kubeadm-init make install-flannel \# Enable kubectl make kubeconfig export KUBECONFIG=$(pwd)/kubeconfig kubectl get pods \-A \# Multi-node make join-command scp join-command another-host:\~/usernetes ssh another-host make \-C \~/usernetes up kubeadm-join |
| :---- |

Agenda: 📑

* [Dragonfly](https://d7y.io/) project updates (P2P) Image distribution \- Gaius

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com)

Notes:

* Dragonfly project  
  * The Dragonfly project provides P2P image distribution for large images  
  * Project has more than 100 contributors.  
  * Nydus (a subproject for Dragonfly)  
    * Provide a content addressable file system on the RAFS format  
    * Enhances the OCI image specification  
    * Reduces the container startup time from minutes to seconds.  
  * Timeline of the project  
    * First version was in 2017  
    * Project was admitted into sandbox in 2018  
    * Incubation project in 2020  
    * 2023 Graduation proposal  
    * One big use case is AI image distribution  
  * Components for the project  
    * Image Acceleration   
    * File distribution  
      * Using P2P technology  
      * Also using Nydus for accelerated images.  
      * Supports distribution protocols: HTTP, HDFS  
      * Support object storage S3, OSS, OBS, etc  
    * AI infrastructure.  
      * Support Triton server and TorchServe  
      * Training \-\> Fluid downloads (dataset) when running on top of JuiceFS  
      * Supports downloading models from Huggingface.  
  * Why use Dragonfly  
    * Kubernetes clusters can have thousands of nodes and images need to be downloaded to each node.  
    * P2P eliminates the bandwidth limitations  
    * Dragonfly also reduces the download size.  
  * Architecture (see presentation and slides)  
    * Components: Manager, Scheduler, Peer  
  * Earlier versions of the scheduler didn't have a filter  
    * New version contains a filter and evaluator to create a DAG tree.  
  * Community is also working on a scheduling solution based on Machine Learning.  
  * Dragonfly also provides deduplication.  
    * Load and chunk deduplication  
  * Best practices  
    * Image acceleration (See slide)  
    * Benchmark \- Clearly better performance than OCIv1 for 50,100,200,500 pods (see slide)  
    * File distribution \- supports large scale distribution.  
    * AI Training \- Works together with Fluid and JuiceFS  
      * It can improve download speeds  
    * AI Inference  
      * Use directly P2P to directly distribute the AI model  
      * Another solution is to use a “Model File System”  
      * Another solution is to use a “Model Image” \- Use an OCI image format.  
      * Can also use plugins: AWS S3, GCS, Azurefile, etc.  
      * TorchServe can use Dragonfly to distribute the model

## [Sept 14th, 2023![][image49]](https://youtu.be/kTG8FuKzGYE)

Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF)

* [Ettore Di Giacinto](mailto:ettore@spectrocloud.com)  
* [Dimitris Karakasilis](mailto:dimitris@spectrocloud.com)  
* [Itxaka Serrano Garcia](mailto:itxak.garcia@spectrocloud.com)  
* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com) \- TAG-Runtime co-chair

Agenda: 📑

* [Kairos](https://kairos.io) project updates ([application](https://github.com/cncf/sandbox/issues/52)) \- [Ettore Di Giacinto](mailto:ettore@kairos.io) [Dimitris Karakasilis](mailto:dimitris@spectrocloud.com) 

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com)

Notes:

* Kairos (an OS distribution factory/engine)  
  * Challenge: Kubernetes at the Edge  
    * Complexity  
    * Managed upgrades  
    * Flexibility  
    * Vendor Neutral  
  * Questions:  
    * What OS do I install?  
    * How do I upgrade it?  
    * How can I scale it?  
    * How can I customize it?  I want to care only about Kubernetes  
  * It’s an immutable Meta Distribution  
    * Vendor neutral (Fedora, Ubuntu, Alpine, etc)  
    * Focused to run Kubernetes (not only)  
    * Highly customizable  
    * Container based  
    * Cloud-init driven  
  * Kairos is Distribution Agnostic  
  * High level overview  
    * Start with a linux container image  
    * Passes through the Kairos factory  
    * Then Kairos images are created with Kairos Core and Kairos Standard (components like K8s or K3s)  
  * The project runs automated tests starting from multiple Linux container images (ubuntu, debian, alpine, rockylinux, alpine, etc)  
  * Kairos Factory  
    * Contains an OCI building engine  
    * It builds the OS from a container image.  
  * They have various ways to do Kairos the installation  
  * It's also easy to configure and manage using the kairos CLI  
  * They also have a tool that is called AuroraBoot to help with fully automated deployments.  
  * They also have an optional peer to peer communication option so that the Kairos nodes can talk to each other. (Information, etc)  
  * Immutability.  
    * The OS is immutable and completely separated from your data.  
      * There is separation between the OS and the user data   
        * User data is persistent (Can also be TPM encrypted)  
  * Kairos allows A/B upgrades (Blue/Green nodes)  
  * It’s also very easy to customize the system image creating a new Dockerfile.  
  * Several ways of managing user data encryption (see diagrams from the presentation). This works for all of the base OSs that they support (SUSE, Ubuntu, etc)  
    * KMS  
    * Offline  
  * Learn more at [https://kairos.io](https://kairos.io)  
  * They leverage the system-upgrade-controller to manage the lifecycle of kairos nodes but they are planning to do their own operator.

* Slides:[https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/19DkDJQXbDIiLobd2oE-EY5pKAX2nzYUMeiGMDv1i2xw/edit\#slide=id.g23f12768656\_2\_53](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/19DkDJQXbDIiLobd2oE-EY5pKAX2nzYUMeiGMDv1i2xw/edit#slide=id.g23f12768656_2_53)

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:ricardo.aravena@gmail.com)

Notes:

* Kubean is a cluster lifecycle management operator based on Kubespray  
* It has declarative API  
* Offline cluster support  
* It also allows customization and extensions.  
* Kubean vs Kubespray  
  * Kubespray provides ansible roles  
  * Kubean uses the Kubespray container image.  
* Kubean vs ClusterAPI  
  * ClusterAPI provides comprehensive range of customizable resources  
  * Kubeban is simpler, just focuses on the cluster lifecycle itself  
* Kubean architecture.  
  * Uses config maps  
    * Ansible inventory  
    * Ansible group vars  
  * Uses a k8s secret to store ssh configs  
  * The operator kicks off Kubespray jobs.  
* Kubean supports many linux distributions.  
* Demo: [https://killercoda.com/Kubean](https://killercoda.com/Kubean)  
* It allows scaling of nodes, upgrading cluster, etc by using the ClusterOperation K8s CRD.  
* Provides customized actions.  
* Can be used for air-gapped deployments/environments.  
* Questions:  
  * \[Rajas\] Is there a potential area of collaboration between kubean and clusterapi  
    * \[Hang\] For now, adoption of clusterapi is not on the roadmap; kubespray is being used  
    * \[Peter\] Kubespray and clusterapi have taken different routes. Kubean will continue with kubespray  
  * \[Rajas\] Has kubean considered joining k-sigs instead of sandbox  
    * \[Xiao\] There have been discussion on this; sandbox is a choice because kubespray focuses on the cluster bootstrap aspect so it fits in the k-sigs org where kubean is an operator so is well suited for sandbox  
  * \[Rajas\] What is the adoption rate for kubernetes minor release?  
    * \[Peter\] The release cadence depends on the kubespray release cadence and in turn on kubernetes release

#### Scribes: ✍️

* Rajas Kakodkar

Notes:

* \[Nikhita\]: Why is a fork of containerd repo needed?  
  * \[Abel\]: Building on the Sandbox API in containerd v1.7, we have introduced an enhanced forked version, which is currently in the containerd 2.0 milestone. However, until this enhanced code gets merged, we require this modified containerd to provide the complete experience  
  * \[Akhil\]: PR for the feature request is open and in the milestone of 2.0  
  * \[Cathy\]: Will the sandboxer API be part of contianerd  
  * \[Linda\]: Kuasar is independent as it not only support containerd but also other high level container runtime, like CRI-O, docker, isulad(already supported)  
* \[Nikhita\]: Is there a plan to support for supporting other wasm runtimes  
  * \[Abel\]: The current release already supports wasmEdge, and the inclusion of wasmtime is part of our roadmap  
  * \[Nikhita\]: Is wasmtime implementation merged? Is it on the roadmap?  
    * \[Abel\]: wasmtime implementation was merged into main branch\! [https://github.com/kuasar-io/kuasar/pull/47](https://github.com/kuasar-io/kuasar/pull/47). Will publish in the next release.  
* \[Nikhita\]: How are the maintainers defined? Maintainers.md has a significant number of maintainers but the github contributors do not show their contributions  
  * \[Abel\]: In addition to code contributions, maintainers are also responsible for community governance, project promotion, and user expansion. Some initial-stage committers do have contributed code. However, the first public commit has squashed all previous commits when the project was published to Github so that certain historical contributions by these committers are incomplete. Despite this, they will follow up on the contribution to the community  
  * \[Cathy\]: Would the maintainers continue contributing?  
  * \[Abel\]: Sure, every maintainer have a specific field to maintain, they will continue to make contributions  
* \[Cathy\]: User adoption for FaaS Platform shows implementation of Wasm Function. Does the function run in a container?  
  * \[Abel\]: It does run in a container defined in the container definition as we want to expand the WebAssembly container to the Kubernetes ecology  
* \[Cathy\]: What is the isolation mechanism for the app kernel?  
  * \[Abel\]: There are different ways of doing isolation.   
  * \[Cathy\]: What is the isolation mechanism for wasm?  
    * \[Abel\]: The isolation relies on the process inside the container can access other resources or not  
* \[Nikhita\]: Are there other adopters of sandbox API?  
  * \[Abel\]: Kuasar is the first and released adopter of the Sandbox API, while other adopters are still in the development phase  
  * \[Burning\]: Sandbox API is experimental in containerd  
* \[Rajas\]: How does the wasm sandboxer compare with runwasi in containerd  
  * \[Abel\]: Not just runwasi, but also kata-shim, firecracker-containerd, and runsc have their own considerations when defining the sandbox. Consequently, their diverse implementations introduce challenges for operations and maintenance engineers to toggle runtimes and identify problems. To address this, we introduce the "sandboxer" concept to simplify the management of different sandboxes and provide some implementations based on popular sandbox  
  * \[Rajas\]: There is a potential possibility for collaboration on the WASM OCI artifacts definition  
* \[Akhil\]: Is the vmm sandboxer process common to all the sandboxers?  
  * \[Abel\]: The single VMM sandboxer process is for all VMM instances belonging to the same sandbox category

* Demo: [https://kuasar.io/blog/kuasar-demo-video/](https://kuasar.io/blog/kuasar-demo-video/)

#### Scribes: ✍️

* Rajas Kakodkar

Notes:  
Slim project update:

- Started as a project to create slim container images  
- Much more capabilities added since then which include  
  - Debugging slim container images  
- Deep dive  
  - [https://github.com/slimtoolkit/slim\#overview](https://github.com/slimtoolkit/slim#overview)   
  - Slim has two components  
    - Sensor  
    - Tmp container  
  - Apart from creating slim container images, it also creates security profiles  
- Discussion:  
  - Hands on experience with slim  
    - Depending on the application, flags have to be configured  
    - 5 Gigs is a good size to start with  
  - Examples on reducing size of fastai image [https://github.com/slimtoolkit/examples/tree/master/3rdparty/python\_fastapi\_official](https://github.com/slimtoolkit/examples/tree/master/3rdparty/python_fastapi_official)  
  - `--include-path` is a common flag [https://github.com/slimtoolkit/slim/tree/master\#usage-details](https://github.com/slimtoolkit/slim/tree/master#usage-details)  
  - Having a dedicated session on advanced uses will help  
- Commands: [https://github.com/slimtoolkit/slim/tree/master\#commands](https://github.com/slimtoolkit/slim/tree/master#commands)  
- `xray` command for security information   
- Depending on how the container image is used, images can be minified using `merge` command  
- `debug` command  
  - Works with docker and kubernetes runtimes  
  - Uses ephemeral containers  
- Goals  
  - Adding more runtime supports which include containerd and podman  
  - Support other tools not limited to docker  
  - Need for improvement in user experience with debugging minimal container images  
- Discussion:  
  - Deep dive on analysis and system calls  
    - System sensor is the crucial component  
    - Runs at the system level and will not be inserted in the container to improve performance   
    - ptrace used for sourcing dynamic information from system calls  
      - Outcome is similar to that of ebpf based monitoring tool  
- Artifacts created by slim include tar of images and container data collected from the analysis  
- Questions:  
  - Image does not shrink  
    - Couple of times it did not work because of the init service used  
    - Process id conflicts with sensor and other systemd services  
    - Another case of failure: System runs out of resources optimizing images when the source image is big. Has worked with 10Gigs and 15Gigs but requires fine tuning of flags apart from the bug which involves including files at runtime  
    - In case of reducing vulnerabilities there can be constraints with reducing size  
    - Most common path: Use default flags and then switch to other flags such `--include-path` `--include-bin` flags in corner cases  
  - Resulting image may not work  
    - Issues with dependencies  
  - Recommended approach: Design the application in a way that the unit/integration tests work with optimized image  
    - Slim runs certain probes  
      - In case of webapps, it would crawl endpoints  
      - Docker exec probes, shell commands/scripts  
      - Container probes, run tests against container image  
      - Setting up integration/e2e  
      - System probes  
  - How does integration with supply chains work with slim removing metadata  
    - One of the gaps is that the minimized image removes metadata so it will not work with supply chain tools  
    - Requires improvement in tools  
    - Slim images are scannable  
    - Goal is to produce SBOM with the required metadata that can work with third party tools  
  - Benchmarks with size differences with slim vs multi stage vs buildpacks  
    - There are a couple of public talks which cover this \[link to be posted\]  
    - User experiences constraints with other approaches  
    - Dependency management   
    - Tradeoffs with complexity with Dockerfiles of multistage builds  
      - Requires knowledge of dependency management   
- Demo on debug command  
- Next steps:  
  - Adding support for WASM based plugins

Annual Reviews for TAGs:

- TOC has been conducting annual reviews, a new process is to get TAG involved to help with annual reviews  
- Akhil, Sean and Alexander can help\!

Container OS working group

- Rajas brought up points that can be included in the scope of the WG  
  - Guidance on cloud native practices \- lifecycle management, container runtimes, considerations around LTS  
  - Flexibility and interoperability with container orchestration solutions  
  - Security  
  - Collaboration between distros  
  - Projects in scope \- flatcar, bottlerocket  
- Rajas will work on the doc and reach out to stakeholders  
  - Sean is willing to help with the doc\!  
- Sean: don’t want someplace where we are all making distros the same  
- Quinton: we should create a common understanding for consumers

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com)

Notes:

* KubeClipper  
  * Lightweight service webui, cli for K8s cluster management.  
  * Provides persistent lifecycle management policies.  
  * The goal of the project is to manage K8s in the lightest most convenient way.  
  * Architecture contains a kc-server and kc-agent.  
  * They also make use of of etcd to store state.  
  * There is support for multi region clusters.  
  * Included support cluster import.  
  * Q. What is the difference between Cluster API and KubeClipper.   
    * It doesn’t use Cluster API or kubeadm.  
    * It has its own CRDs.   
  * Q. How do the provision nodes.  
    * Using the kc-agent installed on the server. (it registers)  
  * They use autok3s  
* Wasmcloud  
  * How the project has evolved since introduced in 2019  
  * One pain point to address improving developer productivity.  
    * Stop the boilerplate code by writing non or less vulnerable code.  
  * It’s a webassembly application runtime (at the heart)  
    * It’s efficient and polyglot  
  * They provide capabilities for cloud native applications: key value stores, load balancers, etc.  
    * Community members are encouraged to implement their own  
  * The core is in Rust (wasm)  
    * There is an sdk in Rust and Tinygo  
  * Deploying  
    * Single binary (in different architectures)  
    * It can run anywhere: K8s, edge devices, VMs, etc  
  * From the beginning it has been a cloud native project  
    * They use the OCI   
    * They use open application spec   
    * Also, cloudevents  
    * Support for open telemetry  
    * They also use NATS to implement the lattice (distributed messaging)  
  * They also publish a container and distribute a helm chart.  
  * Lattice Network  
    * Wasm has the potential to run anywhere, even on the web browser.  
    * It allows all the different services to subscribe to services that are not based on IP addresses.  
    * Devs don’t have to worry about networking  
  * Wasmcloud also is contributing to the webassembly ecosystem including W3c  
  * Under the hood they use the wasmtime runtime  
  * They also prototyping with WASI preview 2  
  * Community  
    * They have a web page  
    * They run weekly community meetings  
    * Anyone is welcome to zoom  
    * They have a list of adopters (the list is growing)  
    * They’ve seen interest grow  
    * Wide range of companies that contribute to wasmcloud  
  * Demo: See meeting recording.

    * Could it be used to clean up things other than container images?  
* KubeMarine  
  * Tool to help manage lifecycle of K8s clusters  
  * It’s a single python binary executable.  
  * It can also be used to deploy a single box Kubernetes  
    * The tool is based on top Kubeadm  
  * Installation can be modified based on a procedure.yaml file  
* [WASM WG update](https://github.com/cncf/tag-runtime/issues/58)  
  * We are looking for Chairs and tech leads. If you are interested, reach out to Heba and state why you would like to be one and possibly how you plan to go about the direction of the WG \- This is the first time we’ve gotten so much interest for a WG so we are working on the logistics.

#### Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF)

* Darshil Parikh  
* Eun Kyng Lee

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com)

#### Agenda: 📑

* [Zot](https://github.com/project-zot/zot): [https://github.com/project-zot/zot/discussions/1067](https://github.com/project-zot/zot/discussions/1067) (onboarding, overview and questions, Ramkumar Chinchani [rchincha@cisco.com](mailto:rchincha@cisco.com))  
  * [https://zotregistry.io](https://zotregistry.io)  
  * You can also reach out at \#zot on CNCF Slack.  
* [Kepler](https://sustainable-computing.io/) project introduction and Cloud native sustainability (Huamin Chen, [hchen@redhat.com](mailto:hchen@redhat.com))

#### Notes: 📓

* Zot is a container image registry  
  * They do releases as binaries on github.  
  * The project is mainly maintained by folks from Cisco  
  * They’ve gotten contributions from many communities.  
  * They’d like to thank the CNCF for being accepted in CNCF  
  * Why did they start the project?  
    * When they went to look for things the OCI community was in its early stages.  
    * Moving forward they decided to go with OCI. That’s where their journey began  
    * There are many container registries, but decided to build their own.  
  * They can help build an OCI native end to end software supply chain.  
  * They get asked a question if they support Docker (they don’t). However, you can use docker to interact with Zot  
  * Zot is an OCI layer manager.  
  * They have a single binary module.  
  * They support multiple platforms \- Linux, MacOS, etc  
  * The way they build the binaries is helpful to reduce the attract surface (with the specific features)  
  * The architecture contains a minimal component and additional extensions.   
  * They support vulnerability checks in the code.  
  * They also support image scanning and singing.  
  * They also support trivy as a backend and they are supporting cross referencing with SBOM (but this is evolving)  
  * They can daisy chain container registries (can also do periodic scan)  
    * This is very similar to git clone.  
  * They also have a search extension.   
    * They’ve added a graphql extension.  
    * They can see images based off of other images.  
    * They can also search by different tags.  
  * They also have a lint extension.  
    * Useful for regulatory compliance.  
  * Scrub extension  
    * Periodic process that verifies image content. Checks for digest, so not affected by bit rot.  
  * Metrics extension  
    * Integrates with the Prometheus stack.  
    * Helpful for the operators for zot. (SREs for example)  
    * Tracks various SLIs  
  * UI extension  
    * Latest release includes the UI.  
  * Use cases  
    * They’ve been using it a Cisco internally  
    * Lot of potential uses  
      * They want to run zot in local systems (very small binary)  
      * They also want to use in embedded systems  
      * Used in CI pipelines too  
      * Zot is also helm registry  
      * Zot has been added to wolfi/os chainguard distribution  
  * Roadmap  
    * Continue to align to OCI standards.  
    * Also, the decisions are based on external cases.  
    * 2.0.0 will be the next release that will include the UI  
  * Comms  
    * They have CNCF slack \#zot channel.  
    * Also github is another channel.  
* Sustainable Computing with Kepler.  
  * What is Kepler about?  
  * They’ve been working a long time with various groups including SIG-storage.  
  * The idea is to track the CPU/Mem consumption and how the workloads consume energy  
  * At the moment they can see energy in pods and containers.  
    * In the future they will support storage, etc  
  * They support x86, ARM, S390x (under dev)   
  * Also uses eBPF to reduce consumption and overhead.  
  * Uses ML models, to do inference on energy consumption.  
  * Kepler components  
    * Has an operator to deploy  
    * Estimator  
    * Model server  
    * Github action  
  * Modeling approach can use different metrics  
    * Examples, motherboard sensor, RAPL, DRAM consumption  
    * ACPI sensor  
    * It can collect metrics through eBPF.  
  * To ensure fairness  
    * Project follows the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHG)  
  * Main module for Kepler is the metrics exporter.   
    * Includes Ratio  
    * Linear regression.  
  * More advanced models  
    * Ie. Linear regression  
      * Model server  
      * Energy estimator.  
  * How does it work?  
    * Selects available metrics like CPU  
    * Then it calibrates idle/energy consumption  
  * Carbonara is used for API.  
  * Project has a documentation page showing all the metrics.  
  *

  * Security Audit: [https://github.com/trailofbits/publications/blob/master/reviews/2023-01-keda-securityreview.pdf?rgh-link-date=2022-09-14T11%3A10%3A21Z](https://github.com/trailofbits/publications/blob/master/reviews/2023-01-keda-securityreview.pdf?rgh-link-date=2022-09-14T11%3A10%3A21Z)

#### Notes: 📓

* KEDA  
  * What has changed since incubation  
  * In the next version 2.11 they will reach out of the box 60 scalers.    
  * They’ve added 33 more scalers  
  * They’ve focused on the authentication providers (They have 9 in total)  
    * Support for major cloud providers  
  * Added support for pausing autocaling  
  * Introduced admission webhooks to enforce autoscaling  
  * Also, started working with TAG Sustainability to measure the impact of scaling.  
    * Looking to integrate with cloud providers to talk to their APIs  
    * In parallel, they are looking to build a standard API.  
  * They started signing container images  
  * They started deploying/creating ARM images.  
  * Support for non public Azure clouds  
  * Security  
    * Container no longer runs as root  
    * Support for custom CA & TLS  
    * Extended security scanning  
    * Completed the security audit  
  * Project wants to be more serious about production  
    * Provide Prometheus operational metrics.  
    * Added off the shelf Grafana dashboards.  
  * Introduced chatops with PRs  
    * More automation to manage contributions  
  * Project also introduced governance.  
    * Scaler governance  
    * Release deprecation, etc  
  * KEDA introduced ability to add scalers in ArtifactHub  
  * Community  
    * 6000+ stars on Github  
    * 260+ contributors  
  * Adoption  
    * 42 listed end users 280% growth since incubation  
    * 11% of K8s users use KEDA  
    * Azure K8s and Openshift are using it.  
  * Question. Do they have any performance test results?  
    * It’s difficult to measure performance because every K8s cluster is different.  
    * They can do basic things.  
    * Suggestion: can we have a baseline of test.  
  * Roadmap  
    * Introduce more scalers  
    * They would like to work/integrate with CloudEvents  
    * First class support for http based scaling  
    * Allow multiple instances of KEDA in a cluster  
    * Make KEDA highly available  
    * Make the ScaledObject configs self-checking  
    * Use OpenTelemetry with scalers  
    * Capability to define autoscaling groups  
    * Plugin ML models to KEDA \-\> Historical or predictive autoscaling  
    * Bring KEDA autoscaling outside K8s (exploring)  
    * Expand collaboration with TAG-Sustainability  
  * Highlights  
    * KEDA can work with other projects like cluster autoscaling  
    * KEDA only focuses on the app

## [March 23rd, 2023](https://youtu.be/mCGvpNSmKyY)[![][image49]](https://zoom.us/my/cncfsigruntime)

#### Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF)

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com)TAG-Runtime co-chair  
* Nikhita Raghunath (VMware)  
* Kevin Wang  
* Hongcai Ren  
* Tiecheng Shen  
* Chauncey Jiang  
* Heba Elayoty

#### Scribes: ✍️

* [Ricardo Aravena](mailto:raravena80@gmail.com)

#### Agenda: 📑

* [Karmada](https://karmada.io/) project update, overview and questions ([kevinwzf0126@gmail.com](mailto:kevinwzf0126@gmail.com))  
  * Slide: [Karmada-Incubation-Application-v5 (1).pptx](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1iLYQzG2uPFY-k4O2KsYOlPfXcbONLoSO/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=117704021223528167287&rtpof=true&sd=true)

#### Notes: 📓

* Background in Karmada. Project want to provide an update before applying for incubation  
* Addressing the challenge of managing multiple clusters with multiple configurations and different parts of the cluster.  
* For example, if a cluster uses custom storage specifically, any change to the cluster might make it unavailable.  
* They feel that K8s native API is very important to manage applications. Folks, don’t want to learn another API. People don’t want to spend more efforts to migrating APIs  
* People also want to be able to have an active-active configuration.  
* Project wants to provide a unified cluster to address networking issues.  
* The architecture allows Karmada to talk to K8s clusters in private and public clouds.  
* When people deploy applications they can use the native K8s manifests  
  * Resource binding provides a unified abstraction for the manifests.  
  * There is also an override policy mechanism if users want to change cluster specific settings.  
* One of the most useful functionalities is the multi-cluster failover.  
  * It helps deploys application across multiple cluster automatically (if there is a failure)  
  * The communication level for applications can be configured to handle different failover scenarios  
* Karmada also has a feature to view all the global resources.  
* From the community perspective.  
  * They think they have very good momentum (over 3000 stars)  
  * More than 50 contributing member organizations (compared to when they entered sandbox)  
* One of the missions of the project is to help end users (and other CNCF projects) easily move to multi-cloud \- multi-cluster architecture  
* Users include banks and CSPs  
* Feedback from the users: They don’t need to adopt a new API \- They can go through directly with what they have already.  
* The project has over 15 adopters   
* There are integrations with many other CNCF projects:  ArgoCD, Flux, OPA, Kyverno, Prometheus, Helm, Istio, Submariner, Velero, KubeEdge, Promtai, CoreDNS, etc.  
* Vivo is an adopter, a company that develops smartphones and accessories. It helps them manage their clusters and scale.  
* ICBC is another adopter \- The largest bank in China.  They have around 100 clusters and Karmada is used to managed 50 clusters  
  * Their use. They think their clusters are vulnerable to failures because of how they have storage configured.  
  * Their clusters are located in different data centers and they want to unify the management.  
  * They also want to expose the underlying resource information like how many clusters they have and how many applications are running on them. While also not providing advanced privilege to access their clusters.   
* China Mobile is another adopter.  
  * They have a large amount of clusters.  
  * They want to use Karmada to deal with the limitation of the cluster sizes. They have heavy workloads.  
  * They also have a lot of stateful applications running (mysql) and they want cluster workloads to talk to each other. Karmada helps them simplify their service access  
* The project had its first release 12/31/2021 by 10/26/2022 Karmada supports 100 large clusters with 5000 nodes each(tested)  
* Future plan is to have wider user adoption and make the community more open to other users. In addition, they expect to do more evangelism especially overseas.   
* They are looking for a TOC sponsor for incubation.

#### Notes: 📓

* Clusternet helps managing K8s cluster locally and remotely  
* Started March 2021 (Open source released 3 months later)  
* The team looked for similar projects in the Cloud Native community but didn’t find any at the time.  
* They have plugin for kubectl to interact directly with clusternet  
* Very easy to migrate from a single cluster controller to multiple clusters  
* It has 3 components: the scheduler (parent cluster), the hub (parent cluster) and the agent (children clusters)  
* The project reuses connections between parent and children clusters to communicate.

* Diane Feddema  
* Huifeng Le  
* Eric Ernst

#### Agenda: 📑

* [Youki](https://github.com/containers/youki) Presentation

#### Notes:

* Container runtime written in Rust  
* Youki in Japanese(容器) means container  
* Good use case for the edge with low footprint \-- 1 mb container can be used for the Edge.  
* Benchmark results: [https://github.com/containers/youki/pull/447\#issuecomment-958991982](https://github.com/containers/youki/pull/447#issuecomment-958991982)  
* It provides a fast startup time.  
* Rust choice helps with the community and system programming.  
* Rust has unique advantages  
  * Memory safety  
  * Static strong typing.  
  * Low level control like C++  
  * Very good and fast FFI   
* Initially with Rust there were some challenges  
  * Initially no OCI spec  
  * Youki came in and helped out  
  * Created: [https://github.com/containers/oci-spec-rs](https://github.com/containers/oci-spec-rs)  
  * In the process of creating a cgroup implementation  
  * They want to create more tools to help the container runtime community.  
* Youki is great for the rust folks to get into the container runtime ecosystem  
  * Also, the container community can learn Rust.  
* They are thinking of using new features like io\_uring to speed up system calls  
  * Also, looking at new features like WASM or Kernel modules

## [**Oct 6th, 2021**](https://youtu.be/KvRM4e4_K8c)[![][image49]](https://zoom.us/my/cncfsigruntime)

#### Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF)

* Alena Prokharchyk (Apple/TOC)  
* Diane Mueller (Red Hat)  
* Roman Mohr (Red Hat)  
* Chris Callegari (Red Hat)  
* Ricardo Aravena (Rakuten)  
* Josh Berkus (Red Hat) (notetaker)  
* Peter Lauterbach (Red Hat)

#### Agenda: 📑

* [KubeVirt](https://kubevirt.io/) Incubation Presentation

#### Notes: 📓

* Kubevirt focuses on seamless integration with Kubernetes  
* It's designed to be very similar to the Kubernetes architecture  
* VMs are mapped to Pods  
* Kubevirt has a control plane designed to work like the Kube control plane  
* VirtualMachineInstance is a normal CRD  
* There's extensions to handle commands/events that aren't covered by pods, like migration  
* Components of Kubevirt architecture each map to part of the kubernetes stack, such as CRI to virt-launcher.  
* (explains architecture diagram)  
* So do you launch the VM with kubectl?  You can, but once the VM is started you need kubectl-virt in order to send VM-specfic commands.  
* Can directly install Kubevirt using the CRD/Operator.  Operator also tries to do some self-healing, and does maint tasks.  
* virt-api handles delegated VM requests, and specific subresources like VNC.  
* Resources tracked by watchers, and there's a controller-manager called virt-controller that actually creates the vm-pods.  
* virt-handler does Privileged operations on the nodes, so it handles (almost) all elevated privs.  
* virt-launcher is a pod that runs the VM, communicates via grpc to virt-handler.  
* (does some looking at the processes that run on a 3-node cluster)  
* Each VM instance has a virt-launcher pod  
* Kubevirt Operator can upgrade Kubevirt itself, "zero-downtime".  Upgrades first node, then controllers, then API so that new features are handled.  
* virt-controller fails over via leader election  
* when you do an upgrade, does the virt-launcher stay up?  Yes, it does, so that the workloads keep running.  upgrading the VMs themselves requires upgrade migration policy.  
* Scaling strategies for virt-api?  You have to define the scale on the operator. Scaling up or down is manual.  Virt-api is stateless so you can have several.  
* What metrics are exposed?  (Roman shares list)  
* Do you have testing for backwards compatibility in upgrades so they don't break?  We use grpc mechanisms for negotiation, and there are upgrade E2E tests for each upgrade.  Upgrade tests run on every PR.  
* They have a large set of E2E tests that run on each PR.  
* Metrics are exposed to Prometheus, including a bunch of VM-specific metrics like CPU and network performance.  Kubevirt looks for Prometheus operator, automatically connects to it.  
* Already using structured logger  
* (some discussion around how finalizers are handled by vm-pods and shutting down vms)  
* Next community health  
  * have governance and contributor ladder, 8 subprojects  
  * try to treat kubevirt as ecosystem more than monolithic project  
  * weekly meeting, summit, Kubecon.  Also participate in other events like ATO and Supercomputing  
  * Eight maintainers, including the original project founders.  Have maintainers from SuSE and Nvidia, Ryan started performance & scale SIG.  
  * Recruiting maintainers?  Chris reaches out to existing contributors from other companies, asks them about increasing their participation. Ryan stepped up end of June.  One staff member from NEC has been contributing a lot and might be headed for Maintainer.  
  * Do you reach out to users?  Yes.    
  * Vasily was promoted after mentorship by the founding maintainers.  
  * Shared statistics on contributors since joining Sandbox  
* DD document has been started. Kubevirt team has been filling in answers.  Will attach recording of this meeting to doc.  
* Video: [https://youtu.be/KvRM4e4\_K8c](https://youtu.be/KvRM4e4_K8c)

#### Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF)

#### Agenda: 📑

* [SuperEdge](https://github.com/superedge/superedge) \- Yiwei Chen, Bobby Zhang (Tencent)  
  * [https://github.com/superedge/superedge](https://github.com/superedge/superedge)

#### Notes:

* Background \-\> Edge computing is growing. The edge computing report from the Linux foundation has specified a reference cloud native stack.  
* Cloud native itself is the motivation for creating SuperEdge  
* Project launched Dec 19, 2020  
  * Extended Kubernetes to the Edge  
  * Tencent was the founding org \-\> Very relevant use cases.  
  * Partnering with Intel, VMware, Huya, Cambricon, Meituan, and CDS  
  * Apache 2.0 license  
* They shared some similar goals to Openyurt but SuperEdge focus is stability  
* K3s is different \-\> Lightweight distribution of K8s  
* KubeEdge has a different philosophy to extend K8s. SuperEdge works based on the requirements of the founding members.  
* The edge has many different types of devices and SuperEdge wants to create a standard way of managing them (also leveraging K8s) \-\> Heterogenous support  
* They want to provide cloud to edge coordination  
* They also want to provide cloud native integration with other things like service mesh, autoscaling, big data/AI.  
* SuperEdge is currently at v0.4.0 (Launched 2 weeks ago)

* Performance benchmark and metrics show better performance than gVisor, and Kata. Similar performance to runc  
* More architectural overview and performance metrics can be found in their repo: [https://github.com/QuarkContainer/Quark](https://github.com/QuarkContainer/Quark)

#### Notes:  📓

* A way to run containers in a secure way without the need to use privileged containers.  
* It’s different from projects like Kata containers and Firecracker in that it doesn’t use a hypervisor  
* Sysbox already gives you a hardened container.  
* Bridges the gap between a container and VM  
* More portable \-\> you don’t need a specific Hypervisor  
* Fully capable of running root in the container.  
* Allows more density, double the capacity compared to VMs

#### Notes: 📓

* Fogflow provides end to end orchestration for AI type of workloads at the edge.  
* It allows you to divide tasks and create a DAG (dependency graph) to orchestrated the tasks  
* It uses “intents’ as triggers for the tasks.  
* It’s programming model uses context driven functions (supports multiple languages)  
* The project is looking at using K8s to run the cloud control module and k3s to run at the edge.   
* The project is part of [Fiware](https://www.fiware.org/) but would be happy to collaborate with the CNCF ecosystem.

## [**October 1st, 2020**](https://youtu.be/vPxPl4MUt2s)[![][image49]](https://zoom.us/my/cncfsigruntime)

#### Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF) 

* Ricardo Aravena  
* Derek McGowan  
* Kevin Hoffman  
* Amye SP (CNCF)  
* Philippe Robin (Arm)  
* Tina Tsou  
* Diane Feddema

#### Agenda: 📑

* WaSCC (Now called [WasmCloud](https://github.com/wasmcloud/)) \- Kevin Hoffman

#### Notes: 📓

- WaSCC has a system of actors and capability providers in WebAssembly  
- These actors and providers can sit anywhere in the network  
- WaSCC uses its own RCP protocol to communicate the actors and providers  
- Actors and providers are decoupled so you can change them on fly without affecting one another (even in production environments)  
- Providers can be anything like radio wave data collectors, or a cloud service like Amazon S3 or a database like Cassandra or Redis.  
- You can write services with minimal code given that you have a set of actors and providers.  
- NATS is used as the message bus for these actors and providers.

## [**September 3rd, 2020**](https://youtu.be/FPH6LPxJ6PA?t=647)[![][image49]](https://zoom.us/my/cncfsigruntime)

Attendance: ✋ (PLEASE ADD YOURSELF)

* Marga Manterola, Alban Crequy, Dongsu Park, Thilo Fromm, Sayan Chowdhury \- Kinvolk  
* Ricardo Aravena \- SIG-Runtime co-chair  
* Sean McCord  \- CyCore Systems  
* Steve Francis

* Amye SP (CNCF)  
* Steven Borrelli 

#### Agenda: 📑

* [Talos](https://github.com/talos-systems/talos)  
* [Flatcar](https://www.flatcar-linux.org/)

#### Notes: 📓

[Talos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FPH6LPxJ6PA&feature=youtu.be&t=716) 🎥

* No general purpose OS  
* Reduce the attack surface, secure the kernel  
* The code is written in Go, auditable in a single place.  
* True read-only image using squashfs  
* Everything is an API (no shell, no ssh, etc)  
* Besides that API access, there are also metrics.  
* Bare minimum to setup with Kubernetes.  
* API is build using GRPC/protobufs  
* No ps \=\> processlist, No cat \=\> readfile (Unix abstracted primitives)  
* High order k8s controllers.  
* Next for Talos  
  * COSI \- Common Operating System Interface  
  * eBPFs \- Eventing, reactive OS  
  * CAPI \- Cluster API providers  
  * Arges \- Manage the complete lifecycle (Sidero \- Baremetal)

[Flatcar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FPH6LPxJ6PA&feature=youtu.be&t=2714) 🎥

* Based on CoreOS, which is based on ChromeOS  
* CoreOS reached its end of life. Kinvolk is developing their own features  
* Flatcar comes from a train (the train that carries containers).  
* Flatcar has 4 channels. Alpha \-\> Beta \-\> Stable and a “labs” channel called Edge  
* Images available in all the cloud providers.  
* Kinvolk Update Service (Nebraska)  
  * Manage the fleet  
  * Operators decide when to update the machine.  
  * Also provides monitoring and visibility.  
* Current Status  
  * Team at Kinvolk maintaining the project.  
  * There is support infrastructure  
  * Broad adoption.  
  * Working on the cluster API integration  
  * Integrating with Rancher.  
* After CoreOS reached end of life and FlatCar continued increased adoption  
* Plans for the future  
  * More updates to the kernel, systemd, etc  
  * eBFP tooling support  
  * Better debugging tools  
  * LTS support in the future (Some people like less updates)

#### Notes: 📓

* [Node Resource Interface](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MVlBXUafB38&feature=youtu.be&t=553) 🎥  
* There are several interfaces in the K8s ecosystem. CRI, CNI, etc  
* There are currently some approaches to address the resources in Kubernetes  
  * CPU manager. UX is a bit clunky  
  * Topology manager. Uses hints.  
* The idea with the NRI is to standardize on some of the existing mechanisms  
  * Leverage CNI style configuration   
  * Leverage CNI style plugins  
* Use Konfine tool \- K for Kubernetes  
* Some of the existing tools could evolve into plugins (CPU Manager, etc)  
* Next steps  
  * Formal spec  
  * Demo some plugins  
  * Containerd implementation with ctr  
* Proposal will be presented to sig-node  
* Next steps from SIG, identify potential leads to drive this initiative or through time let it develop organically.

#### Agenda: 📑

* [Lupine presentation](https://www.eurosys2020.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/slides/159_kuo_slides.pdf) (Dan Williams, [djwillia@us.ibm.com](mailto:djwillia@us.ibm.com))  
  * Paper: [https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3342195.3387526](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3342195.3387526)

#### Notes: 📓

* KubeEdge DD  
* Lupine  
  * Research at IBM on containers, VMs and unikernels  
  * Containers are great for running apps, etc.  
  * Typical deprivilization is using Virtual Machines (widely acknowledged)  
  * An approach for deprivivilization is unikernels  
    * Downside is that they don’t support multiprocessors  
    * Nabla containers on top of rumprum is a step to containerize unikernels  
  * Lupine  
    * Address  
      * Want to be able multi-processor  
      * Want to run linux workloads  
    * Issue with unikernels  
      * They don’t support all apps  
      * Communities curate applications  
    * Use the standard linux kernel but specialized\!  
    * With 19 kernel config options it can run about 20 or the most popular container apps

* Quay  
* Container Registry with no vendor dependencies.  
* Releases always go to quay.io first.  
* Working on OCI Compliance Test reference  
* Driving OCI standards.  
* Several features  
  * Claire image scanning  
  * Image builder support  
  * Multiple storage providers (on-prem, AWS, Azure, GCP, etc)  
  * Prometheus metrics  
  * Enterprise RBAC support  
  * Notary integration

  * Image time machine allows users to roll back their tag.

* Project is addressing every layer so that they have redundancy.  
* Contains a comprehensive test suite.

* Ford has a use case for centralized registry to handle a lot of applications

  * Support air-gapped deployment  
  * Deeper integration w/K8s

* [Kata Containers](https://katacontainers.io/) Intro (by Tao Peng)  
  * Lightweight VM isolation and individual kernels for your workloads  
  * Have a running container inside a microVM within a couple of seconds  
  * Uses containerd to integrate with CRI (kubelet) and created containerd-shim-kata-v2 to simplify and reduce \# of components for each sandbox

## [**March 19th, 2020**](https://youtu.be/vRfuhT6-u18)[![][image49]](https://zoom.us/my/cncfsigruntime)

* Diane Feddema (dfeddema@redhat.com)  
* Klaus Ma ( @k82cn )  
* Samuel Ortiz

#### Agenda: 📑

* Virtual Kubelet Incubation  
  * Speaker: Ria Bhatia (@rbitia)  
  * Issue: [https://github.com/cncf/sig-runtime/issues/12](https://github.com/cncf/sig-runtime/issues/12)  
  * PR: [https://github.com/cncf/toc/pull/296](https://github.com/cncf/toc/pull/296)  
*  SIG-Runtime Roadmap Discussion  
  * [https://docs.google.com/document/d/17cEUZ-vkZm0awKzHKWMfSh4H8HQwv-ksd2fItKV2HS8](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17cEUZ-vkZm0awKzHKWMfSh4H8HQwv-ksd2fItKV2HS8)

#### Notes: 📓

* Virtual Kubelet  
* Virtual Kubelet created to understand capacity  
* Initially worked with hyper.sh  
* Made it more extensible, allow folks to create providers  
* With 1.0 others can create providers, better for decoupling  
* 5 contributors, 33 releases, etc.  
* Now more in maintenance mode.  
* Netflix uses virtual kubelet on top of Mesos (Titus) \- Good talk at last Kubecon  
* VK has providers and it puts a lot of responsibility on the providers  
  * Create pod  
  * Get pod status  
  * Etc  
* Elotl has been creating a provider, the goal is to have as much conformance as possible.  
* VK uses toleration to deploy

#### Recap:📝

* VK team will come back with some more documentation (initially at a high level) about what APIs work and what APIs don’t.  
  * Quinton: [Here](https://github.com/cncf/toc/pull/296#issuecomment-535717796) are the previous requests for clarification that I repeated in the meeting, most notably:  
    * Brian Grant, Sept 26, 2019: “ I'd want to see documentation of what it supports and what its limitations are at a comparable level of detail and rigor as Windows support in Kubernetes”.  
    * Brian Grant, Oct 1, 2019: “Substantial technical due diligence is required when a project enters incubation, whether it was previously in Sandbox or new to CNCF. Such diligence is not possible without a clear indication of what works and what doesn't, and what is underway and what won't ever work.”  
* We will discuss roadmap items in the next meeting
